newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Moslem headscarf row divides coalition.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Moslem headscarf row divides coalition.

text.p: An Islamist proposal to allow Turkish women civil servants to wear Moslem headscarves at work has rekindled a decade-old dispute and divided secular Turkey's ruling coalition.

Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, modern Turkey's first Islamist leader, has mostly steered clear of introducing Islamic norms into public life since his Welfare Party (RP) gained power in a coalition with the conservative True Path Party (DYP) last June.

But in the current Moslem fasting month of Ramadan, he has revived pledges for a mosque in Taksim Square -- a bar and cinemas district in Istanbul's secularist centre -- introduced shorter workdays for civil servants wishing to break their fast at sundown and promised to allow headscarves in state offices.

"If the Welfare Party brings proposals that we can in no way approve or accept and becomes insistent about it, this will bar the continuation of the coalition," conservative Health Minister Yildirim Aktuna told Turkish television late on Tuesday.
Under current legislation, Turkey can discipline women civil servants for wearing the headscarf and sack them for repeated offences. University rectors can forbid the headscarf at their discretion.

"A change in the law is well overdue," Esma Urun, head of the RP Ladies' Commission in the party stronghold of Konya, told Reuters. "In Turkey, people should be able to live according to their beliefs. People say Turkey is becoming European, but it is way behind Europe on secularism and freedom of belief."

The Turkish republic was founded as a strictly secular state by Kemal Ataturk in 1923 from the crumbling Islam-based Ottoman Empire. Turkey's secularists, most notably the powerful army, are wary of any move they see as a return to Ottoman values.
RP members deny the latest plans are a bid to set up a strict Islamic state.

"On the contrary, these moves will make society more tolerant," senior RP deputy Salih Kapusuz told reporters. "It is not possible for us to condone a prohibitive mentality. Our basis is human rights, and we will not take any steps back."
"Promoters of sharia (Islamic law) are making great progress in taking the country into the darkness of the Middle Ages," said Hikmet Cetinkaya, editor of the leftist Cumhuriyet daily.
The civil servants' dress code, which requires women to have their hair uncovered and combed, was introduced in the years following a coup in 1980 under the military then in charge.
Welfare women say the rule has bred Islamic radicalism. Many say they were moved to join the party by its "oppression".

Leman Aksay, a chemical engineering graduate and former head of the RP Ladies' Commission, said earlier that she boycotted university for a year after being ordered to remove her scarf. Because of the scarf, she was offered only lowly state-sector jobs. The private sector would not take her on at all.

Welfare says it did not field any women candidates in the last elections because, if elected, they would be barred from entering parliament in their Islamic dress -- usually a scarf, long sleeves and long skirt, or a long coat.

Gulsen Ataseven, a practising doctor who wears a headscarf, attacked the dress code as a way to insult the devout and leave women ignorant by keeping them out of school. She said it contravened international rights agreements signed by Turkey.

"It is just one insult after another," Ataseven told Reuters. "Everywhere in the world they are trying to get more women educated and here they are putting barriers before them. As it is, ignorance will grow and we will see more Fadimes."

Ataseven, who heads an Islamist women's group in Istanbul, was referring to a recent scandal in which 21-year-old Fadime Sahin complained she was tricked into sleeping with a Moslem sect leader to "free the evil spirits that invaded her body".
